sentences.text: Oohkotokia was a large, heavily built, four-legged herbivore reaching up to 5 meters in length and weighing up to 2 metric tons.
Its skull resembles those of Euoplocephalus but is distinguished by a relatively smooth overall surface texture compared to other ankylosaurids of the same era.
This dinosaur possessed a tail club made of bone plates permeated with soft tissue capable of absorbing thousands of pounds of force.
The name Oohkotokia means "child of stone" in reference to the dinosaur's extensive body armor, derived from a Blackfoot word and a Latin suffix.
A partial skull once referred to Dyoplosaurus but now associated with Oohkotokia features very large squamosal horns and unique Z-shaped tooth carinae.
The genus Oohkotokia contains the single type species Oohkotokia horneri, which was named and described in 2013 by Paul Penkalski.
Paul Penkalski described the genus Oohkotokia after rediscovering a specimen in the collection of Montana's Museum of the Rockies that had been stored for over three decades.
Researchers suggest the large tail clubs of Oohkotokia may have been used for self-defense against predators or rivals, or for sexual selection.
Oohkotokia shared its habitat with diverse fauna including oviraptorosaurs, ornithopods, nodosaurs, ceratopsians, Troodon, dromaeosaurids, and tyrannosauroids.
The crushed condition of the Oohkotokia skull suggests it was damaged by dinoturbation, the trampling of bones by passing dinosaurs.
Oohkotokia is classified as a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur belonging to the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.
Paul Penkalski assigned Oohkotokia to the subfamily Ankylosaurinae based on skull anatomy and body armor morphology.
Oohkotokia fossils are known from the upper levels of the Two Medicine Formation in Montana, dating to about 74 million years ago during the late Campanian stage.
Studies suggest Oohkotokia lived in a seasonal, semi-arid environment with possible rainshadows from the Cordilleran highlands.
